danish.title: Femte bog (1806–07) — Kapitel 10
paragraphs: Kort efter sin optagelse i Frimurerbroderskabet rejste Pierre til provinsen Kiev, hvor han havde det største antal livegne, og medbragte udførlige anvisninger, som han selv havde skrevet ned til sin egen vejledning om, hvad han skulle gøre på sine godser.

Da han nåede Kiev, kaldte han alle sine forvaltere til hovedkontoret og forklarede dem sine hensigter og ønsker. Han sagde dem, at der straks ville blive taget skridt til at frigive hans livegne — og at de indtil da ikke måtte overbelastes med arbejde, at kvinder, der ammede deres børn, ikke måtte sendes på arbejde, at der skulle ydes hjælp til de livegne, at afstraffelser skulle være formanende og ikke korporlige, og at der på alle godser skulle oprettes hospitaler, asyler og skoler. Nogle af forvalterne (der var halvt analfabetiske opsynsmænd iblandt dem) lyttede med rædsel, idet de antog, at den unge greves ord betød, at han var utilfreds med deres forvaltning og underslæb af midler; andre blev efter den første forskrækkelse morede over Pierres udtalefejl og de nye ord, de ikke havde hørt før; atter andre nød blot at høre, hvordan herren talte, mens de klogeste blandt dem, herunder overforvalteren, af denne tale forstod, hvordan de bedst kunne håndtere herren til egen fordel.
Overforvalteren udtrykte stor medfølelse med Pierres intentioner, men bemærkede, at ud over disse ændringer var det nødvendigt at se på den generelle tilstand, som langtfra var tilfredsstillende.

Trods grev Bezukhovs enorme formue følte Pierre sig, efter at han var kommet i besiddelse af en indtægt, der sagdes at beløbe sig til fem hundrede tusind rubler om året, langt fattigere, end da hans far havde givet ham et underhold på ti tusind rubler. Han havde en dunkel fornemmelse af følgende budget:

Omkring 80.000 gik til betalinger på alle godserne til Jordbanken, omkring 30.000 gik til vedligeholdelse af godset nær Moskva, byhuset og apanagen til de tre fyrstinder; omkring 15.000 blev givet i pensioner og lige så meget til asyler; 150.000 blev sendt som underholdsbidrag til grevinden; omkring 70.000 gik til renter på gæld. Opførelsen af en ny kirke, der var påbegyndt tidligere, havde kostet omkring 10.000 i hvert af de sidste to år, og han vidste ikke, hvordan resten, omkring 100.000 rubler, blev brugt, og næsten hvert år var han nødt til at låne. Desuden skrev overforvalteren hvert år til ham om brande og misvækst eller om nødvendigheden af at genopføre fabrikker og værksteder. Så den første opgave, Pierre stod over for, var en, han havde meget lidt anlæg og tilbøjelighed for — praktisk forretningsførelse.

Han drøftede godsanliggender med sin overforvalter hver dag. Men han følte, at det ikke bragte noget fremad overhovedet. Han følte, at disse drøftelser var løsrevne fra de virkelige forhold og ikke hængte sammen med dem eller satte dem i bevægelse. På den ene side fremstillede overforvalteren sagerne i det værst mulige lys og fremhævede nødvendigheden af at betale gælden af og påtage sig nye aktiviteter med brug af livegent arbejde, hvilket Pierre ikke kunne gå med til. På den anden side krævede Pierre, at der blev taget skridt til at frigive de livegne, hvilket forvalteren imødegik ved at påpege nødvendigheden af først at betale lånene til Jordbanken af og den deraf følgende umulighed af en hurtig frigørelse.

Forvalteren sagde ikke, at det var helt umuligt, men foreslog at sælge skovene i provinsen Kostroma, jorden længere nede ad floden og godset på Krim for at gøre det muligt: alt sammen transaktioner, der ifølge ham var forbundet med så indviklede foranstaltninger — ophævelse af forbud, ansøgninger, tilladelser og så videre — at Pierre blev helt forvirret og blot svarede:
»Ja, ja, gør det.«

Pierre havde ingen af den praktiske udholdenhed, der ville have sat ham i stand til selv at tage sig af forretningerne, og derfor brød han sig ikke om det og forsøgte blot at lade, som om han passede det, over for forvalteren. Forvalteren på sin side forsøgte at lade, som om han fandt disse drøftelser meget værdifulde for ejeren og besværlige for ham selv.

I Kiev fandt Pierre nogle bekendte, og fremmede skyndte sig at gøre hans bekendtskab og bød med glæde den rige nytilkomne, provinsens største godsejer, velkommen. Fristelserne til Pierres største svaghed — den, han havde bekendt ved sin optagelse i Logen — var så stærke, at han ikke kunne modstå dem. Igen gik hele dage, uger og måneder af hans liv i et lige så stort jag og var lige så optaget af selskaber, middage, frokoster og baller, der ikke levnede ham tid til eftertanke, som i Petersborg. I stedet for det nye liv, han havde håbet at føre, levede han stadig det gamle, blot i nye omgivelser.

Af frimureriets tre forskrifter indså Pierre, at han ikke opfyldte den, der pålagde enhver frimurer at sætte et eksempel med et moralsk liv, og at han af de syv dyder manglede to — moralitet og kærlighed til døden. Han trøstede sig med tanken om, at han opfyldte en anden af forskrifterne — at reformere menneskeslægten — og besad andre dyder — kærlighed til sin næste og især gavmildhed.

I foråret 1807 besluttede han at vende tilbage til Petersborg. Undervejs ville han besøge alle sine godser og med egne øjne se, i hvor høj grad hans ordrer var blevet udført, og i hvilken forfatning de livegne var, som Gud havde betroet ham, og som han agtede at gavne.

Overforvalteren, der betragtede den unge greves forsøg som næsten vanvittige — ufordelagtige for ham selv, for greven og for de livegne — gjorde visse indrømmelser. Han fortsatte med at fremstille frigørelsen af de livegne som uigennemførlig, men arrangerede opførelsen af store bygninger — skoler, hospitaler og asyler — på alle godser, inden herren ankom. Overalt blev der gjort forberedelser, ikke til ceremonielle velkomsthilsener (som han vidste, Pierre ikke brød sig om), men netop til sådanne taknemmeligt religiøse modtagelser med overrækkelse af ikoner og brød og salt, som efter hans forståelse af sin herre ville røre og narre ham.

Det sydlige forår, den behagelige, hurtige rejse i en wiener-karet og vejens ensomhed havde alle en oplivende virkning på Pierre. De godser, han ikke før havde besøgt, var det ene smukkere end det andet; de livegne syntes overalt at trives og var rørende taknemmelige for de velgerninger, der var tilfaldet dem. Overalt var der modtagelser, der ganske vist bragte Pierre i forlegenhed, men vakte en glad følelse dybt i hans hjerte. Ét sted overrakte bønderne ham brød og salt og en ikon af Sankt Peter og Sankt Paul og bad om tilladelse til som tegn på taknemmelighed for hans velgerninger at opføre et nyt kapel ved kirken for egen regning til ære for Peter og Paul, hans skytshelgener. Et andet sted mødte kvinderne med spædbørn på armen ham for at takke ham for at have fritaget dem for hårdt arbejde. På et tredje gods kom præsten, bærende et kors, ham i møde omgivet af børn, som han med grevens velvilje underviste i læsning, skrivning og religion. På alle sine godser så Pierre med egne øjne murstensbygninger, der var rejst eller under opførelse, alle efter én plan, til hospitaler, skoler og alderdomshjem, der snart skulle åbne. Overalt så han forvalterens regnskaber, ifølge hvilke de livegnes hoveriarbejde var blevet formindsket, og hørte de rørende taksigelser fra deputationer af livegne i deres langskødede blå kofter.

Hvad Pierre ikke vidste, var, at stedet, hvor de overrakte ham brød og salt og ønskede at bygge et kapel til ære for Peter og Paul, var en markedslandsby, hvor der blev holdt marked på Sankt Peters dag, og at de rigeste bønder (der udgjorde deputationen) længe før havde påbegyndt kapellet, men at ni tiendedele af bønderne i den landsby levede i den største fattigdom. Han vidste ikke, at da ammerne ikke længere blev sendt på arbejde på hans jord, arbejdede de stadig hårdere på deres egen. Han vidste ikke, at præsten, der mødte ham med korset, undertrykte bønderne med sine opkrævninger, og at elevernes forældre græd over at lade ham tage deres børn og sikrede deres frigivelse mod store betalinger. Han vidste ikke, at murstensbygningerne, der var opført efter plan, blev bygget af livegne, hvis hoveriarbejde derved var forøget, skønt det på papiret var formindsket. Han vidste ikke, at der, hvor forvalteren i regnskaberne havde vist ham, at de livegnes betalinger var nedsat med en tredjedel, var deres obligatoriske hoveriarbejde forøget med en halvdel. Og således var Pierre henrykt over besøget på sine godser og genvandt helt det filantropiske humør, hvori han havde forladt Petersborg, og skrev begejstrede breve til sin »broder-vejleder«, som han kaldte Stormesteren.
»Hvor let det er og hvor lidt anstrengelse det kræver at gøre så meget godt,« tænkte Pierre, »og hvor lidt opmærksomhed vi skænker det!«
Han glædede sig over den taknemmelighed, han modtog, men skammede sig over at modtage den. Denne taknemmelighed mindede ham om, hvor meget mere han kunne gøre for disse enkle, venlige mennesker.

Overforvalteren, en meget dum, men udspekuleret mand, der så den naive og intelligente greve helt igennem og legede med ham som med et stykke legetøj, pressede ham endnu hårdere med beviser for umuligheden og frem for alt nytteløsheden af at frigive de livegne, der var ganske lykkelige, som de var.

Pierre var i sin inderste sjæl enig med forvalteren i, at det ville være svært at forestille sig lykkeligere mennesker, og at kun Gud vidste, hvad der ville ske med dem, når de blev frie, men han fastholdt, omend modvilligt, det, han anså for rigtigt. Forvalteren lovede at gøre alt, hvad der stod i hans magt, for at opfylde grevens ønsker, da han klart indså, at greven ikke blot aldrig ville være i stand til at kontrollere, om alle foranstaltninger var truffet til salg af jorden og skovene og til frigørelse fra Jordbanken, men sandsynligvis aldrig engang ville spørge og aldrig ville få at vide, at de nyopførte bygninger stod tomme, og at de livegne fortsat indbetalte i penge og arbejde alt, hvad andre ejeres livegne indbetalte — det vil sige alt, hvad der kunne presses ud af dem.

english.title: Book Five (1806 - 07) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Soon after his admission to the Masonic Brotherhood, Pierre went to the Kiev province, where he had the greatest number of serfs, carrying with him detailed instructions he had written for his own guidance on what to do with his estates.

When he reached Kiev, he summoned all his stewards to the head office and laid out his intentions and wishes. He told them that steps would be taken immediately to free his serfs — and until then, they were not to be overworked, nursing mothers were not to be sent to labor, assistance was to be given to the serfs, punishments were to be educational rather than physical, and hospitals, asylums, and schools were to be established on all the estates. Some of the stewards — among them semi-literate foremen — listened with alarm, supposing these words meant the young count was unhappy with their management and their embezzlement. Some, after their initial fright, were amused by Pierre's lisp and the unfamiliar words. Others simply enjoyed hearing the master talk. But the cleverest among them, including the chief steward, understood from this speech exactly how to manage the master for their own benefit.

The chief steward expressed great sympathy with Pierre's plans, but pointed out that besides these changes it would be necessary to review the overall state of affairs, which was far from satisfactory.

Despite Count Bezukhov's enormous wealth — since he had come into an income reportedly amounting to five hundred thousand rubles a year — Pierre felt himself far poorer than when his father had given him an allowance of ten thousand. He had a rough sense of the following budget:

About 80,000 went in payments on all the estates to the Land Bank; about 30,000 for the upkeep of the Moscow estate, the town house, and allowances to the three princesses; about 15,000 in pensions and the same for asylums; 150,000 in alimony to the countess; about 70,000 for interest on debts. Construction of a new church, previously begun, had cost about 10,000 in each of the last two years, and he didn't know how the rest — about 100,000 rubles — was spent. Almost every year he had to borrow. Besides this, the chief steward wrote annually about fires and bad harvests, or about the need to rebuild factories and workshops. So the first task Pierre faced was one for which he had very little talent or inclination — practical business.

He discussed estate affairs every day with his chief steward, but felt that none of it moved anything forward. He sensed that these consultations were disconnected from real life and didn't make things happen. On one hand, the chief steward painted the worst possible picture, emphasizing the need to pay off debts and undertake new projects with serf labor — to which Pierre wouldn't agree. On the other hand, Pierre demanded that steps be taken to liberate the serfs, which the steward deflected by pointing out that the Land Bank loans must be paid off first, making immediate emancipation impossible.

The steward didn't say outright that it couldn't be done, but suggested selling the forests in Kostroma province, the land along the lower river, and the Crimean estate — all of which involved, according to him, such complicated procedures — injunctions, petitions, permits, and so on — that Pierre became thoroughly bewildered and could only reply:
"Yes, yes, do that."

Pierre lacked the practical persistence needed to manage the business himself, so he disliked it and only pretended to the steward that he was paying attention. The steward, for his part, pretended to the count that these consultations were extremely valuable for the proprietor and troublesome for himself.

In Kiev, Pierre encountered some people he knew, and strangers rushed to make the acquaintance of the rich newcomer, the largest landowner in the province. Temptations targeting Pierre's greatest weakness — the one he had confessed at his Lodge initiation — were so powerful that he couldn't resist them. Once again whole days, weeks, and months passed in a blur of evening parties, dinners, lunches, and balls, leaving him no time for reflection — just like in Petersburg. Instead of the new life he had planned, he was living the same old life, only in different surroundings.

Of the three Masonic precepts, Pierre realized he was failing the one that required every Mason to set an example of moral living, and of the seven virtues he lacked two: morality and the love of death. He consoled himself with the thought that he was fulfilling another precept — reforming humanity — and possessed other virtues: love of his neighbor and especially generosity.

In the spring of 1807 he decided to return to Petersburg. On the way, he planned to visit all his estates and see for himself how his orders had been carried out, and what condition the serfs were in — the serfs God had entrusted to his care and whom he intended to help.

The chief steward, who considered the young count's schemes nearly insane — unprofitable for himself, for the count, and for the serfs — had made some concessions. While continuing to represent the liberation of the serfs as impractical, he arranged for large buildings — schools, hospitals, and asylums — to be erected on all the estates before the master arrived. Everywhere preparations were made, not for ceremonious welcomes (which he knew Pierre wouldn't like), but for touchingly religious ones, with offerings of icons and the bread and salt of hospitality — just the kind that, in his understanding of the master, would impress and deceive him.

The southern spring, the comfortable, rapid travel in a Viennese carriage, and the solitude of the road all had a cheering effect on Pierre. His estates — which he had never visited before — were each more picturesque than the last; the serfs everywhere seemed thriving and touchingly grateful for the benefits conferred on them. Everywhere there were receptions, which, though they embarrassed Pierre, stirred a joyful feeling deep in his heart. In one place the peasants presented him with bread, salt, and an icon of Saints Peter and Paul, and asked permission — as a mark of gratitude — to build a new chapel at their own expense in honor of his patron saints. In another, the women with babies came to thank him for releasing them from hard labor. On a third estate, the priest came to meet him bearing a cross, surrounded by children whom — thanks to the count's generosity — he was teaching reading, writing, and religion. On all his estates Pierre saw brick buildings either completed or under construction, all built to the same plan, for hospitals, schools, and almshouses — which were due to open soon. Everywhere he saw the stewards' accounts showing that the serfs' compulsory labor had been reduced, and heard the grateful speeches of deputations of serfs in their best blue coats.

What Pierre did not know was this: the place where they presented him with bread and salt and wanted to build a chapel in honor of Peter and Paul was a market village where a fair was held on Saint Peter's Day, and that the richest peasants (who made up the deputation) had started building the chapel long before; nine-tenths of the peasants in that village were in extreme poverty. He did not know that since the nursing mothers were no longer sent to work on his land, they now did even harder work on their own. He did not know that the priest who met him with the cross was squeezing the peasants for fees, and that the pupils' parents wept at having to give up their children, paying heavily to get them back. He did not know that the brick buildings, built to a uniform plan, were being constructed by serf labor — increasing their workload, even though it had been reduced on paper. He did not know that where the steward's accounts showed a one-third reduction in the serfs' payments, their obligatory estate labor had been increased by half. And so Pierre was delighted with his visit to his estates and wrote enthusiastic letters to his "brother-instructor," as he called the Grand Master.
"How easy it is, how little effort it takes, to do so much good," thought Pierre, "and how little attention we pay to it!"
He was pleased by the gratitude he received but felt awkward about it. The gratitude reminded him of how much more he could do for these simple, kind people.

The chief steward — a very stupid but cunning man who saw right through the naive and intelligent count and played him like a toy — observing the effect of these staged receptions, pressed him even harder with arguments about the impossibility and especially the pointlessness of freeing the serfs, who were perfectly happy as they were.

Pierre secretly agreed with the steward that it would be hard to imagine happier people, and God only knew what would happen to them when they were free — but he insisted, though reluctantly, on what he believed was right. The steward promised to do everything in his power to carry out the count's wishes, knowing perfectly well that not only would the count never check whether the forests had actually been sold or the Land Bank loans paid off, but would probably never even ask — and would never find out that the newly built buildings stood empty and that the serfs continued to hand over, in money and labor, everything that could be squeezed from them.
